candidate.answerReason: There are exactly 27 allowable planes. Covering the 36 required face segments requires at least seven planes, and three central squares together with four central hexagons attain that bound.

methods.label: Classify the sections and prove both bounds
methods.explanation:
On each face, the four edge midpoints determine six required segments: two join opposite edge midpoints, and four join adjacent edge midpoints. Call these midlines and corner segments, respectively. Altogether there are \(12\) midlines and \(24\) corner segments.

An allowable plane cuts each face it crosses in a straight chord. Since no additional surface points are allowed, that chord must be one of the six required segments. Also, every required segment must lie in at least one chosen plane: finitely many planes that do not contain its line could cover only finitely many points of the segment.

We first classify all allowable planes. Choose coordinates so the cube is \([-1,1]^3\). This merely chooses a convenient common scale.

Suppose a section contains a midline. By cube symmetry, take that midline to have endpoints \((0,-1,1)\) and \((0,1,1)\). On the adjacent face \(y=1\), the section must join \((0,1,1)\) to one of that face's other three edge midpoints:
\[
(0,1,-1),\quad (1,1,0),\quad (-1,1,0).
\]
Three noncollinear points determine a plane, so these choices give, respectively,
\[
x=0,\qquad x+z=1,\qquad -x+z=1.
\]
The first produces a central square; the other two produce rectangles. Applying cube symmetry gives exactly three central squares and twelve rectangles. Each rectangle has midlines on exactly two adjacent faces, and there is one such rectangle for each of the cube's twelve edges. Each square contains four required face segments, while each rectangle contains four, including two midlines.

Now suppose a section has no midline. Take one of its corner segments to have endpoints \((1,0,1)\) and \((0,1,1)\). On the face \(x=1\), its next segment must join \((1,0,1)\) to either \((1,1,0)\) or \((1,-1,0)\); the third possible endpoint would create a midline. These choices determine
\[
x+y+z=2
\quad\text{or}\quad
x+y-z=0.
\]
The first cuts off a corner triangle, giving eight possibilities, one for each cube vertex. The second gives a central hexagon. Its symmetric versions have equations \(\pm x\pm y\pm z=0\); reversing all signs gives the same plane, so there are \(2^3/2=4\) hexagons. These triangles and hexagons have only required corner segments as their sides.

The classification is exhaustive, and each listed plane is allowable. Thus at most
\[
3+12+8+4=27
\]
planes can be chosen.

To bound the minimum, let \(t\) be the number of chosen planes containing midlines. Each covers at most four of the twelve midlines, so \(t\ge3\). Such planes meet only four faces; every other plane meets at most six. Covering all \(36\) required segments therefore requires
\[
36\le4t+6(k-t)=6k-2t\le6k-6,
\]
which gives \(k\ge7\).

Seven planes do suffice. The three central squares cover all twelve midlines. The four central hexagons cover all twenty-four corner segments: on \(z=1\), their traces are exactly \(x+y=\pm1\) and \(x-y=\pm1\), and the same holds on every other face by symmetry. Hence the minimum is \(7\). Adding all remaining allowable planes introduces no extra surface points, so the maximum is \(27\).

The requested difference is
\[
27-7=\boxed{20},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
